questiontext.text:
Goal

Write three small classes, each defining a different combination of __repr__ and __str__.

How this works in Python

Java gives an object one way to describe itself, and one audience to describe itself to.

class Sensor {
    private final String code;
    private final double reading;

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "Sensor[code=" + code + ", reading=" + reading + "]";
    }
}

System.out.println(sensor);            // calls toString
System.out.println(List.of(sensor));   // calls toString on each element

Python splits that one method into two, because the two audiences want different things.

  • __repr__ is for a developer holding a broken program. Make it precise, show the real values, and aim for text you could paste back into the source.
  • __str__ is for a person reading output. Make it readable, and leave out whatever the reader does not need.

Which one Python calls depends on how you ask. print(sensor), str(sensor) and f"{sensor}" all go to __str__. repr(sensor) and f"{sensor!r}" go to __repr__.

A container prints the repr of its contents, never the str

print([sensor]) calls __repr__ on the sensor inside, and so does a tuple, a dict and a set. This catches everybody once. You write a lovely __str__, print a list of your objects, and get something else entirely.

The fallback runs one way only. Write __repr__ alone and print uses it, because __str__ falls back to __repr__ when you have not written one. Write __str__ alone and a list of your objects still prints rubbish. That is why __repr__ is the one to write first, and often the only one worth writing.

Write neither and Python prints this.

<__main__.Sensor object at 0x7f2a1c0d3ef0>

A class name and a memory address. It is Java's Sensor@6d06d69c and it is worth the same, which is nothing. The address changes on every run, so it cannot even go in a bug report.

One piece of syntax carries the weight here. {self.code!r} inside an f-string is the !r conversion from the strings topic. It formats the value with repr rather than str, so a string keeps its quotes and you can see that "3" is not 3. Use it on every value inside __repr__.

def __repr__(self) -> str:
    return f"Sensor(code={self.code!r}, reading={self.reading!r})"
Your task

Write three small classes. None of them prints anything by itself.

  • Sensor(code, reading) stores both values under those names. Its __repr__ returns Sensor(code='S1', reading=21.5) and its __str__ returns sensor S1 reading 21.5.
  • Reading(code, value) stores both values under those names and has __repr__ only, returning Reading(code='R7', value=3). Leaving __str__ out is the point of this one.
  • Bare(code) stores the code and has neither dunder. Leave it useless on purpose, and read what the tests print about it.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Do not write a method named toString. Nothing in Python will ever call it.
  • Define __repr__ above __str__ inside Sensor, and use !r on both values inside it.
  • Give Reading no __str__ and give Bare neither dunder. A hidden test checks that you left them out.
  • Annotate every signature. __init__ returns -> None, __repr__ and __str__ return -> str, and self is never annotated.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

testcode.text: one = Sensor("S1", 21.5) two = Sensor("S2", 4.0) print(one) print(repr(one)) print([one, two])

expected.text: sensor S1 reading 21.5 Sensor(code='S1', reading=21.5) [Sensor(code='S1', reading=21.5), Sensor(code='S2', reading=4.0)]

testcode.text: only = Reading("R7", 3) print(only) print(repr(only)) print([only]) print(f"{only} and {only!r}")

expected.text: Reading(code='R7', value=3) Reading(code='R7', value=3) [Reading(code='R7', value=3)] Reading(code='R7', value=3) and Reading(code='R7', value=3)

testcode.text: import inspect sensor_src = inspect.getsource(Sensor) assert "def toString" not in sensor_src, "rule broken: that name is Java. Write __repr__ and __str__" assert "!r" in sensor_src, "rule broken: use the !r conversion inside __repr__" assert sensor_src.index("__repr__") < sensor_src.index("__str__"), "rule broken: __repr__ comes first" assert "def __str__" not in inspect.getsource(Reading), "rule broken: leave Reading with no __str__, that is what it is for" plain = Bare("B4") text = repr(plain) print(text.startswith("<__main__.Bare object at 0x"), text.endswith(">"), str(plain) == text) print(str(Sensor("S3", 0.5)), "|", repr(Sensor("S3", 0.5)))

expected.text: True True True sensor S3 reading 0.5 | Sensor(code='S3', reading=0.5)

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write two classes and a function that show what __eq__ does to a class's hash.

How this works in Python

Java has a contract you have broken at least once. Override equals and you must override hashCode as well. Nothing enforces it.

@Override
public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (!(o instanceof Tag other)) return false;
    return kind.equals(other.kind) && number == other.number;
}
// no hashCode. This compiles. This ships.

That class works everywhere except a HashSet or a HashMap, where two equal tags land in different buckets and the set holds both. Nothing throws. The wrong answer arrives quietly, months later, in production.

Python renames the pair and then does something Java never does.

equals becomes __eq__

The == operator calls it. The signature is __eq__(self, other: object) -> bool, and other is annotated object because anything at all can turn up on the far side of ==. You get != free, because Python derives it from __eq__. Never write __ne__.

__eq__ deletes your hash

This is the part with no Java equivalent, and it is the whole point of this tier. The moment a class defines __eq__, Python sets that class's __hash__ to None. Your objects stop being hashable.

{tag}
# TypeError: unhashable type: 'Tag'

Read that as Python refusing to let you ship the Java bug. Rather than let a half-kept contract rot in a set, it breaks the class the first time anyone tries, loudly, on the developer's own machine. Put the hash back yourself.

def __hash__(self) -> int:
    return hash((self.kind, self.number))

Hash a tuple of the same fields that __eq__ compares. The contract is Java's contract. Two objects that compare equal must hash equal. Hash only fields that cannot change while the object sits in a set, because an object whose hash moves is an object you cannot find again.

Return NotImplemented for a stranger, never False

When other is not your type, you do not know the answer. Say so. NotImplemented is a built-in constant, and returning it tells Python to ask the other operand instead. Only when both sides decline does Python fall back to identity and answer False.

def __eq__(self, other: object) -> bool:
    if not isinstance(other, Tag):
        return NotImplemented
    return (self.kind, self.number) == (other.kind, other.number)

Answer False there instead and you have ruled on behalf of a type you have never seen. A wrapper that knows perfectly well how to compare itself to a Tag never gets asked. isinstance is Python's instanceof, and NotImplemented is not NotImplementedError. One is a value you return and the other is an exception you raise.

Your task

Write two classes and one function.

  • Tag(kind, number) stores both values under those names. Give it __repr__ returning Tag(kind='valve', number=7), __eq__ comparing both fields and returning NotImplemented for a stranger, and __hash__ over both fields.
  • Loose(label) stores the label, defines __eq__ the same way, and deliberately has no __hash__. It exists to break.
  • unhashable_error() puts a Loose into a set inside a try, catches the TypeError, and returns its message as a string.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Do not write a method named equals or hashCode. Write the dunders Python actually calls.
  • Do not write __ne__. Python derives != from __eq__, and writing it by hand is how the two drift apart.
  • Return NotImplemented when the other operand is a stranger. Never return False there.
  • Hash a tuple of the same fields __eq__ compares.
  • Leave Loose with no __hash__. A hidden test checks that you did.
  • Annotate every signature. __eq__ takes other: object, __hash__ returns -> int, and self is never annotated.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI for explanation only. Ask it what an error means or why one form is more idiomatic. Do not let it write your answer.

testcode.text: one = Tag("valve", 7) same = Tag("valve", 7) other = Tag("pump", 7) print(one == same, one is same, one == other) print(one != same, one != other) print(len({one, same, other})) counts = {one: 3} print(counts[same])
one = Tag("valve", 7) print(one == "valve7", one == 5, one == None) print(one.__eq__("valve7") is NotImplemented) print(Loose("x") == Loose("x"), Loose("x") == "x") print(unhashable_error())

expected.text: False False False True True False unhashable type: 'Loose'

testcode.text: import inspect tag_src = inspect.getsource(Tag) for banned in ("def equals", "def hashCode", "def __ne__"): assert banned not in tag_src, "rule broken: Python does not want that method" assert "NotImplemented" in tag_src, "rule broken: return NotImplemented for a stranger" assert "def __hash__" in tag_src, "rule broken: put __hash__ back yourself" assert "def __hash__" not in inspect.getsource(Loose), "rule broken: leave Loose with no hash, that is what it is for" print(hash(Tag("valve", 7)) == hash(Tag("valve", 7))) print({Tag("a", n) for n in range(3)} == {Tag("a", 2), Tag("a", 1), Tag("a", 0)}) print(sorted({Tag("a", 1), Tag("a", 1), Tag("b", 1)}, key=lambda tag: tag.kind))

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write a value class by hand, then build a second one with a dataclass and an enum instead.

How this works in Python

A Java value object costs you four methods before it does any work. toString, equals, hashCode and compareTo. Python has the same four jobs under different names. One of the four behaves in a way Java never warns you about.

toString splits in two

Python asks for __repr__ and __str__. __repr__ is for you while you are debugging, so make it precise and show the real values. __str__ is for a person reading output. Print an object and Python calls __str__. Print a list of objects and Python calls __repr__ on each one. Leave __repr__ out and the list prints <__main__.Batch object at 0x7f9c...>. That line tells you nothing. Write __repr__ first. Use the !r conversion from the strings topic inside it so strings keep their quotes.

def __repr__(self) -> str:
    return f"Batch(code={self.code!r}, readings={self.readings!r})"

equals becomes __eq__, and it deletes your hash

In Java, overriding equals without hashCode compiles cleanly and then fails at run time, because the object never comes back out of a HashSet. Python stops you sooner. Defining __eq__ sets __hash__ to None, so your object raises TypeError the moment you put it in a set. Put the hash back yourself, and hash only the fields that cannot change. Hash a list and an object could move buckets while it still sits in a set. Preventing that bug is why Python deletes the hash in the first place.

Return NotImplemented for a stranger

When the other operand is not your type, do not return False. Return the built-in constant NotImplemented, which tells Python to ask the other object instead. Only when both sides decline does Python fall back to identity and answer False. It is not the same thing as NotImplementedError, and it is not raised. The example below asks about the other operand with isinstance. That function is Python's instanceof.

def __eq__(self, other: object) -> bool:
    if not isinstance(other, Batch):
        return NotImplemented
    return (self.code, self.readings) == (other.code, other.readings)

compareTo becomes __lt__

Define less-than and sorted() works. Three more dunders make your object behave like a container. __len__ powers len(), __iter__ powers a for loop, and __contains__ powers the in keyword. Iterable[int] is anything you can loop over and Iterator[int] is what __iter__ hands back, and both names come from collections.abc rather than from typing.

Now delete most of it. A Java record writes the value-object half for you, and Python's answer is the dataclass.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field, replace

@dataclass(frozen=True, order=True, slots=True)
class Sample:
    code: str
    readings: list[int] = field(default_factory=list, compare=False)

Each line in the class body names a field and annotates its type, in the annotation style from the type hints topic. Python still checks nothing at run time. The decorator reads those annotated names anyway and writes __init__, __repr__, __eq__ and the ordering dunders. Three switches matter here. frozen=True blocks assignment after construction and raises FrozenInstanceError. order=True writes the comparison dunders. slots=True drops the per-instance dictionary. That saves memory and blocks attributes you never declared.

A dataclass goes further than a record in four ways you need here.

  • Defaults. A record has none. A dataclass field can have one.
  • field(default_factory=list). Write readings: list = [] instead and the decorator raises ValueError before your program runs. A bare [] there would be one list shared by every instance. That is the shared mutable from the classes topic again, caught this time by the library. default_factory takes a function and calls it once per instance.
  • compare=False. Keeps a field out of equality and ordering.
  • __post_init__. The generated __init__ calls it after every field is set, which is where validation goes.

Copy a frozen instance with a change using replace(sample, code="S9"). Be careful with the word frozen. The freeze is shallow. The instance refuses new attribute values, but a list stored inside it still accepts append.

Last, the loose string constant. Java gives you an enum and a switch over it. Python gives you Enum, and auto() supplies the values so you never write them.

from enum import Enum, auto

class Severity(Enum):
    LOW = auto()
    HIGH = auto()

Each member is a single object that exists once, so compare members with is, never with their underlying value. Loop over the class and you get the members in definition order. You already built the dispatch half of a Java switch in the closures topic. It is a dict of functions, and now the keys are enum members.

Your task

Write both halves. Build Batch by hand, then let the decorator build Sample for you.

  • Batch, built by hand, taking code and readings. Store a copy of the readings with list(readings). Give it __repr__, __str__, __eq__, __hash__, __lt__, __len__, __iter__ and __contains__. __str__ returns f"batch {code} holding {..} readings". Order on code alone.
  • Severity, an enum with LOW and HIGH from auto().
  • Sample, a dataclass built with @dataclass(frozen=True, order=True, slots=True). It has three fields in this order. code comes first. severity comes next, defaulting to Severity.LOW with compare=False. readings comes last, with a default_factory and compare=False. __post_init__ raises ValueError(f"code {code!r} must be 1 to 4 characters") when the code length is outside 1 to 4.
  • mutable_default_error() defines a broken dataclass inside a try, catches the ValueError, and returns its message as a string.
  • shallow_freeze() builds Sample("S1", Severity.HIGH, [1, 2]), appends 3 to its readings, then tries to assign a new code inside a try. Return f"{readings} but code is frozen: {..}" with the list and the caught exception's type name.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Do not write a method named equals, hashCode, toString or compareTo. Write the dunder Python actually calls.
  • Define __repr__ above __str__. A hidden test checks the order, because a list of your objects prints the repr.
  • Define __hash__ yourself. __eq__ has already deleted the inherited one.
  • Hash only fields that cannot change, and say why in one comment.
  • Return NotImplemented when the other operand is a stranger. Never return False there.
  • Do not write __init__, __repr__, __eq__ or __lt__ inside Sample. The decorator writes all four.
  • Do not give any dataclass field a mutable default. Use field(default_factory=..).
  • Raise in __post_init__. Never clamp a bad value quietly into range.
  • Compare enum members with is. Never compare their values.
  • Annotate every signature you write. __eq__ takes other: object, because anything at all can turn up on the other side of ==.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.

name.text: WAT 19.4: Java in a Python Suit!

questiontext.text:
Goal

Rewrite an AI's Java-shaped class and its three callers as idiomatic Python.

This one is a code review. The class below was written by an AI, it is already in the starter box, and every visible test passes.

Here is what it wrote. Read it before the explanation.

class Station:
    def __init__(self, name: str, altitude: int) -> None:
        self.set_name(name)
        self._altitude = altitude

    def get_name(self) -> str:
        return self._name

    def set_name(self, value: str) -> None:
        if value == "":
            raise ValueError("name must not be empty")
        self._name = value

    def get_altitude(self) -> int:
        return self._altitude

    def to_string(self) -> str:
        return "Station " + self._name + " at " + str(self._altitude) + "m"

    def equals(self, other: object) -> bool:
        if not isinstance(other, Station):
            return False
        return self._name == other._name and self._altitude == other._altitude

Three functions sit below the class and they are the callers. Their results must not change by a single character, but they carry the same accent as the class.

def describe(stations: list[Station]) -> list[str]:
    lines = []
    for station in stations:
        lines.append(station.to_string())
    return lines


def rename(station: Station, value: str) -> str:
    station.set_name(value)
    return station.get_name()


def count_distinct(stations: list[Station]) -> int:
    seen = []
    for station in stations:
        found = False
        for other in seen:
            if station.equals(other):
                found = True
        if not found:
            seen.append(station)
    return len(seen)
How this works in Python

Passing tests is not the same as the code being right

Tests check behaviour. They say nothing about whether the next person can read the code, whether the shape belongs in the language, or whether a caller has to learn a private vocabulary before touching your object. At work you will be reviewing AI-written Python in a safety-critical codebase, where a green suite is the beginning of the review rather than the end of it. This question is that review, on a small scale.

Every line runs. The annotations are correct. There is no bug in it. It is a Java class transliterated word for word, with the Java kept and the Python left out, and the giveaway is that not one of those six methods has a name Python itself will ever call.

get_name and set_name

The classes topic already retired the getter that only hands a field back. The rule there was to expose the attribute, because Python has no private fields to guard and no reason to route a plain read through a method call. That kills get_altitude outright, and altitude becomes an ordinary attribute.

set_name is the interesting one, because it does something. It rejects an empty name, and that check has to survive. Wrap the pair in a property and you keep the check while the caller writes station.name = "Bluff". The @property decorator marks the reader, and @name.setter marks the writer.

@property
def name(self) -> str:
    return self._name

@name.setter
def name(self, value: str) -> None:
    if value == "":
        raise ValueError("name must not be empty")
    self._name = value

Both are called name, and that is not a mistake. The setter attaches itself to the property the reader created. Once both exist, __init__ can assign self.name = name and the check still runs, which is where the Java version had to remember to call its own setter by hand.

to_string

Python calls __str__. Nothing in the language will ever look for a method named to_string, so print(station) prints a memory address today and always will. Build the text with an f-string rather than gluing five pieces together with + and a call to str().

equals

Python calls __eq__, so one == two is False here no matter what the fields hold. Rename it, and fix the stranger case while you are in there. Return NotImplemented rather than False. Then remember what __eq__ does to the hash and put __hash__ back, or the rewritten count_distinct cannot use a set.

describe builds a list with a loop and append where a comprehension belongs. count_distinct compares every station against every other one, which is the loop you write when your objects cannot go in a set. Once __eq__ and __hash__ are in place, that whole function is len(set(stations)).

Your task

Rewrite the class and all three functions so they read as Python. The visible tests check the behaviour has not moved. The hidden test checks the Java shape is gone, so a rewrite that keeps the old names fails even though the output is right.

  • Station, rewritten. name becomes a property whose setter keeps the empty-name check, and altitude becomes a plain attribute.
  • __str__, __eq__ and __hash__ on Station, in place of to_string and equals.
  • describe(stations), rewritten with a comprehension.
  • rename(station, value), rewritten against the property.
  • count_distinct(stations), rewritten with a set.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Leave no method whose name begins get_ or set_, and none named to_string or equals. The hidden test looks for all four.
  • Give name a property whose setter keeps the empty-name check. Make altitude a plain attribute, because its getter never did anything.
  • Write __str__ with an f-string. No + and no call to str().
  • Write __eq__ returning NotImplemented for a stranger, then put __hash__ back after it.
  • Build describe with a comprehension and count_distinct with a set. Write no append anywhere.
  • Keep every return value exactly as it is today. This is a rewrite, not a redesign.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed for discussion. The code below came from an AI and it passes every test. Your job is to judge it, so do not ask an AI whether it is good.

testcode.text: north = Station("Kaitaia", 3) south = Station("Bluff", 8) print(describe([north, south])) print(rename(north, "Kaitaia North")) print(describe([north]))

expected.text: ['Station Kaitaia at 3m', 'Station Bluff at 8m'] Kaitaia North ['Station Kaitaia North at 3m']

testcode.text: one = Station("Kaitaia", 3) two = Station("Kaitaia", 3) three = Station("Bluff", 8) print(count_distinct([one, two, three])) print(count_distinct([])) try: rename(one, "") except ValueError as problem: print("ValueError:", problem) try: Station("", 12) except ValueError as problem: print("ValueError:", problem) print(describe([one]))

expected.text: 2 0 ValueError: name must not be empty ValueError: name must not be empty ['Station Kaitaia at 3m']

testcode.text: import inspect whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(item) for item in (Station, describe, rename, count_distinct)) for banned in ("get_", "set_", "to_string", "equals"): assert banned not in whole, "rule broken: a Java name is still there" assert ".append(" not in whole, "rule broken: a comprehension and a set do that work" assert "def __hash__" in whole, "rule broken: __eq__ deleted the hash, so put one back" assert "NotImplemented" in whole, "rule broken: return NotImplemented for a stranger" assert "__str__" in Station.__dict__, "rule broken: Python calls __str__, not to_string" text_src = inspect.getsource(Station.__str__) assert 'f"' in text_src or "f'" in text_src, "rule broken: build the text with an f-string" assert isinstance(Station.__dict__.get("name"), property), "rule broken: name must be a property" assert Station.__dict__["name"].fset is not None, "rule broken: the property needs a setter that keeps the check" assert "altitude" not in Station.__dict__, "rule broken: altitude is a plain attribute, because its getter did nothing" one = Station("Kaitaia", 3) two = Station("Kaitaia", 3) print(str(one)) print(one.name, one.altitude) print(one == two, one == "Kaitaia", one.__eq__("Kaitaia") is NotImplemented) print(len({one, two})) one.name = "Kaitaia West" print(one.name)

expected.text: Station Kaitaia at 3m Kaitaia 3 True False True 1 Kaitaia West
